newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's star judge defends bold election bid.
newsitem.headline: Italy's star judge defends bold election bid.

text.p: Former star anti-graft magistrate Antonio Di Pietro on Thursday defended his decision to run for parliament on a centre-left ticket, a move which has exposed cracks in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition.
Di Pietro, a former public works minister in the Prodi government, announced on Wednesday night he would run for a Senate seat in a Tuscan district about to become vacant.
But the decision by the ex magistrate, who became a folk hero because of his Milan-based Mani Pulite (Clean Hands) probes of corruption in the early 1990s, caused a political storm.

Di Pietro, who left the magistrature in December 1994 for reasons that have never fully been explained, is himself currently under investigation by magistrates in the city of Brescia on suspicion of alleged irregularities while he was a magistrate.

The Brescia magistrates had already cleared Di Pietro of several accusations of corruption. They are currently probing allegations that his wife, a lawyer, received gifts and loans from a leading Italian constructor.
The constructor, Antonio d'Adamo, was linked to a banker Milan magistrates had investigated for corruption.
A number of supporters of Prodi's coalition said they were against the move.

"There was no need for this ... this was a senseless decision. This is madness," said Fausto Bertinotti, whose hard-left Communist Refoundation party shores up Prodi's majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
In an interview with Italian television on Thursday, Di Pietro blasted his critics, including those in the Prodi coalition under whose centre-left umbrella he will run.
He said he was throwing his hat into the ring to help usher in constitutional reforms due to be discussed by parliament.
Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi, himself the subject of probes by Milan magistrates when he was prime minister, accused Di Pietro of seeking election to cover himself from prosecution.
"The mask is off -- a strange magistrate with a habit of running up debts has decided to seek parliamentary immunity. I wish him luck," Berlusconi said.
Although Italian parliamentarians no longer enjoy immunity from investigation they still enjoy some legal privileges.
Under a 1993 law magistrates no longer have to ask parliament to probe MPs but they still must seek permission to arrest a member, tap a telephone or search a home or office.

"You can't offer a parliamentary seat and the immunity that derives from it to a person who has just been been caught up in a judicial storm," said Mauro Paissan, head of the Greens in the lower house of parliament.
Di Pietro hit back in Thursday's television interview.
"Parliamentary immunity does not exist any more," he said, adding that by the time the election was held, the investigation in Brescia would have run its course.
Di Pietro said the accusations against him would turn out to be false and promised to withdraw his candidacy if investigating magistrates ask for his indictment.
"I am sure this will not happen, that is why I am putting forward my candidacy now," he said.
